Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople

Photius, Archbishop of Constantinople: Oration on the Birthday of the Most Holy Theotokos

Every feast and every festal assembly that brightens the gathering of the devout puts an end to the quarrels and disputes people have with one another. It brings together those who stand apart in their opinions, and those who have broken the bond of affection through faction. By the harmony of its hymns it offers in practice an appeal to come back to concord. It also shows that those gathered there are creatures and works of one and the same Master and Creator. By the unity of their worship it reveals that all were made with equal honour, and so it softens and humbles those who bitterly exalt themselves over one another. It persuades them to think modest and human thoughts, and teaches them to look to the same hand of the Maker and to remember the same clay from which they were fashioned. To my mind at least, this is why the ordinance fitting for Christians prescribes the celebration of festivals. One festival shows Christ being born; another bears witness to his baptism; another presents him transfigured; another shows him working divine signs: healing the demon-possessed, giving sight to the blind, drying up fountains of blood, strengthening the lame and the paralysed, raising the dead. Another finally sets him before us hanging on the cross, and another again shows him rising and inaugurating my own resurrection by deeds that are seen. Every festival worthy of God thus gives us the enjoyment of the gifts we share, and each also shines with its own particular radiance of grace. But the present festival, which honours the birth of the Virgin and Mother of God, carries off the prize far above all the others. We know that the root is the cause of branches and trunk, of fruit and flower. All the effort and toil spent on the rest may be for the sake of the fruit, yet none of the others springs up without the root. In the same way, without the Virgin's festival

none of the festivals that sprang from it would appear. There is a resurrection because there was a death; a death, because there was a crucifixion; a crucifixion, because Lazarus came up from the gates of Hades on the fourth day, because the blind see, because the paralytic runs carrying the bed on which he lay, and because of the other wondrous works. This is not the moment to list all the rest. The Jewish nation ought to have glorified and praised them, but instead they inflamed it to envy, and out of that envy it plotted against the Saviour to its own destruction. These things happened because Christ was baptized, freed humanity from error, and taught the knowledge of God by deed and by word. There was a baptism because there was a birth, and the birth of Christ came about, to put it briefly and well, because the Virgin was born. In her birth we are made new, and we have been counted worthy to celebrate it. So the Virgin's festival plays the part of root, or spring, or foundation, or whatever more fitting word I might find. It is rightly made glorious by all those other feasts, it is distinguished by many great gifts, and it is known as the day of the whole world's salvation. For today the Virgin Mother is born of a barren mother, and the palace is made ready for the Master's sojourn among us. Today the bonds of barrenness are loosed, and the bars of virginity are sealed. A sterile womb, dead to every means of bearing children, brought forth a lovely fruit beyond all hope, and by these same means the incorruption of virginity is betrothed and the wonder of the conception is foretold by manifest deeds. A birth without a man and virginity kept intact after childbirth are beyond nature. But a barren woman who is tilled after old age and gives birth also overcomes the laws of nature, and by the wonders through which this is done it serves as a prelude to the Virgin's own childbearing. Today Anna mows down the reproach of childlessness, and the world reaps the ears of joy. Joachim is called the father of a child, and we receive the pledge of the dignity of adoption. Today the Virgin comes forth from barren loins, barrenness takes the place of the offspring of sin, the fullness of the synagogue of the Jews is widowed, and the children of the Church's bosom peep forth, growing and multiplying for Christ the bridegroom in a manner worthy of God. The Virgin comes forth from barren loins whose childbearing would have been a marvel even if they had been fertile. O what a wonder! When the time for sowing had passed, then the season for bearing fruit arrived. When the fire of desire had been quenched, then the lamp of childbearing was lit. Youth bore no flower, and old age puts forth a shoot. No swelling belly was known while nature was in its prime, and from a womb long past its prime an ever-virgin babe is revealed as offspring. But are you at a loss, O man, over whether a barren woman has given birth?

Or rather, using the very things that should make you marvel as they make us marvel, do you seek to belittle the marvel and argue over how a barren woman could give birth? For if a barren woman does not give birth, and a woman who gives birth is not barren, how do breasts that had dried up open into springs of milk? If old age cannot store up blood, how do the nipples turn into milk what they never received? How does a deadened womb bring an embryo to completion, give it life, hold it and nourish it? You contrive these arguments against yourself and against your own salvation. Who are you? You cannot be one of the faithful, of those worthy of the wonder, for a believer will never be brought to disbelieve the very things through which faith exists. No, you are a Jew. Then how, or where, did Sarah slip your mind? Did she not see Isaac as the child of old age and barrenness? Is it Anna who confuses and troubles your reasoning, or rather Sarah, since she came first? If this is what perplexes you, then you are the one who fails to see that you are cancelling your own kinship and cutting off the roots from which you have your being as a branch, and you stand convicted of having fallen away from the Jewish ordinances. Now if I said that the birth came about in the ordinary course of nature and then urged you to agree, barrenness, old age and nature would rightly have given birth to the labour of your syllogisms [?]. But if I proclaim the event as a work of divine grace, why do you force grace to be the slave of nature, when grace has always been nature's mistress? Do you accept Adam, fashioned from clay and brought into being without birth? Do you accept Eve, who came to exist without union as the offspring of a rib? You could not give an account of these things in terms of nature. The growth and birth of human beings by succession keeps to a different order of coming into being, so it does not allow us to regard their production as a work of nature. Nor again is it contrary to nature, for it is the beginning of the natural constitution of human beings. It belongs, then, to the divine will and power. Well then? In that case you grant that the Divine has power even over the more marvellous things, and you do not arm the order of nature against its Maker. But now, as though you had condemned that all-powerful and pure power to a deep old age, do you declare it weaker in these matters? Trained by the earlier examples, you ought rather to have been seen offering others an unwavering faith about them. So the one who disputes this would not be a Jew, if he really were a Jew, but one of those who have a Greek mind and outlook. Do you then disbelieve and scorn the idea that a child came forth from a barren woman, you who make men the children of rot? You who made dragon's teeth the very wombs of your ancestors? Would that you showed me their tombs while you say this! You who command stones to become human, and who trace the genealogy of your forefathers' race in a way worthy of yourself, back to the blood of ants! You hold these views, even though they are long-winded drivel, and you have nothing whatever, no grace, no mind,

no nature, no perception, no one else's opinion, not even your own, nothing else at all to plead for them except your own shamelessness or stupidity. Yet you cherish and champion them. Meanwhile there are things that even conflicting opinions confirm, compelled by the truth to speak with one voice about them. Their first witnesses are eyesight and perception, and many similar events of long ago lend them credence even apart from what has been said. These are the things you try to mock and dismiss as worthless! I would not say that we need to dignify our own beliefs by the absurdities those people have championed. Far from it. Light is not made bright by darkness, truth is not established by falsehood, and faith is not supported by error. My point is that they had no right at all, having sunk so utterly low (as far below as we are raised above nature), to honour and admire things that are contrary to nature and could not be put together in any way, while trying with argument and error to shake things far greater than reason and nature, things of relief [?], to which even now the tombs of the martyrs bear witness by working wonders when need calls and Providence arranges it. Consider this too. Does passion not overpower nature? Does disease not? Old age? Does not youth itself, at the very height of its bloom, become a weakness for begetting, if anything does? And here is a paradox, if familiarity did not steal away our astonishment: the very thing through which a man comes to be a father keeps him, for a time, from becoming one. What then? The passions overpower nature, though they are nothing but an affection and excess of it. Will grace not overpower the nature it fashioned, if it wishes? Old age chills and dries up the springs of seed, and will the Maker not warm and water what has grown old? Nature easily bears those conditions to which it has not yet been brought down, before their time has come, and which are worse than those toward which it is being dragged. Will the Maker not readily bring it back, if he wishes, to the bounds he set for it from the beginning? Do you disbelieve what I have said? Very well. These fine transformations of yours that I am about to list are not mine, far from it. Or rather, it is for you to list them, so that you may have more to boast of over us in your most edifying tales. Tell of the poplars that came from human beings, from whose eyes flows the amber of the myth, with which you enrich your silliness. Count the laurels too, and the palm trees, the nightingales and the swallows, your singing swans and halcyons, and your kindly dolphins. Sing of your androgynous Tiresiases, so that they may settle a quarrel of the gods worthy of their licentiousness. By allotting the greater share of pleasure to the goddess, they reaped harm from their frankness.

Shall I also remind you of the bulls that cross the sea, steered by love for an unhappy maiden? Of the long journeys abroad, the many wanderings, and the sojourns far from Olympus? I pass over the rest in silence. It is not fitting to mix the filth of error with the myrrh of faith, or to outrage the rays of piety with the deep gloom of impiety. So let us bid a long farewell to the long drivel and the myths. We pity those infatuated with them for their folly, and hate them for their arrogance. Let us now steer back to the course our discourse set at the beginning. Long ago, then, human nature had been enslaved to the power of ancestral sins, and the birth of the descendant, trumpeting the coming of the one who would destroy them, gave bright signs that we would recover from tyranny and be freed from slavery. That is why Adam and Eve, cleansed of the ancient stains of their transgression and having shaken off their gloomy dejection, rejoice and lead the dance of the Virgin's festival with free voice and countenance; or rather, they stand at its head. The seed of sin spread through the whole race through them and corrupted it, so now that sin is being uprooted, they are rightly the ones to begin the joy and the dance, and to go out and call together those born from them. The sickness of the fall flowed from the first transgressors through all, and all needed the same cure. Today the salvation of the whole world is founded on the Virgin's birth. So it was fitting to hold a festival common to the whole race, and to strike up public songs of thanksgiving that rise above this world, for a salvation that embraces the whole world demands a thanksgiving beyond the world. Let us send up songs of thanksgiving, because Adam is refashioned, Eve is renewed, and the curse is dissolved. Our nature puts off the dead, leathern mask of sin and is reshaped to the ancient dignity of the Master's image. Let us send up songs of thanksgiving and form choirs of all the people, because the Virgin, peeping forth from a barren bosom, sanctifies the barren womb of nature, grafting its unfruitfulness into a rich harvest of virtues. She lent the streams of her undefiled blood to the Master and Husbandman of all, to water the whole lump of humanity that had dried up, and so she rightly receives in return the blessing of fruitfulness. The ladder that leads up to heaven is being set in place, and earthly nature leaps over its own bounds and takes up residence in the heavenly mansions. The Master's throne is prepared on earth, and earthly things are sanctified. The ranks of heaven gather together with us, and the evil one, who first deceived us and became the architect of the plot against us, has his strength broken as his tricks and devices crumble.

Who will be able to recount the wonders of God? What words will express things whose power is beyond words? How will every mind not grow numb as it stretches its understanding to match the greatness of these works? In the beginning God fashioned man, moved by the unspeakable wealth of his love for humanity. Man was the work of his own hand, graced to bear the image of the one who fashioned him; one aspect showed the nobility of the flesh, the other that of the spirit. A paradise, a delightful and lovely thing, had been planted in the east [?]. It was fragrant with the unfading flowers of meadows and rich with the ripe fruits of every kind of plant. Rivers flowed through its midst and watered the face of the plain with their pure streams, giving the place an indescribable beauty. Here the Maker settled the masterpiece of his sovereign hand. He made him master of all and showed him surrounded by an abundance of every good thing. Then, by an ineffable delivery, he brought forth a companion from his side, so that she would know the one from whom she was taken, the one who had lent her her being, as her head. She would look to him and remember her debt, and alongside the bond of nature a bond of concord would dwell between them. He granted them the enjoyment and mastery of everything in paradise. But the one entrusted with so vast an authority had to be trained and tested by some commandment, so God brought in a law for him that was neither hard to live by nor altogether too easy to keep, and by it reward or liability would be decided. From among the plants blooming in beauty he set one apart from the others by his word, and gave a commandment forbidding them to eat of that one alone. But a wicked beast, the originator of evil, whom his own deeds named the devil, had eyed man with envy from the moment he was fashioned. He used another beast, one of the creeping things, as his instrument. He spoke alluring and bewitching words to the woman, poured out much blasphemy against the lawgiver, and persuaded the woman, and through her her husband, to disregard the commandment and eat what they had been forbidden to eat. And the moment they transgressed the command, they fell away from all the gifts, which was exactly what the schemer was striving for. His whole device had been built for this end. From then on the transgression was sown from the ancestors into their descendants, and the schemer held our whole race enslaved under his hand. What, then, of the Maker and Guardian? Did he forever overlook his creature in its misery, sunk in so great an error and enslaved by the passions day after day? Not at all. How could he gladly bear to see what he had fashioned with such zeal carried off as plunder and led astray? So the unity of the Trinity took counsel with itself, if one may put it so. And one may say this of the refashioning, since the words "Let us make man in our image and likeness" were said of the original fashioning. By the single will of its purpose

it arranged the refashioning of the shattered creature. Humanity had grown terribly savage and desolate, and could not be brought back by threats, punishments, laws or prophets. So this purpose sought a man who shared our nature, in whom one could see the law kept without a single breach. Then humanity, seeing one of its own race living that way, could imitate its kinsman. And through the very means by which the contriver of the devices had bound his power upon us, he would be cast down from his lordship by a lawful victory and contest. So one of the Trinity had to be numbered among men, so that the refashioning might be seen to belong to the one to whom the original fashioning belonged. And that one had to be the Son, so that he would bear this title below without outraging the dignity above, since he was the Son and was glorified as such from eternity. But to be numbered among the sons of men was impossible without incarnation. Incarnation is the road to birth, and birth is the completion of pregnancy. Pregnancy implies a mother, and so rightly demands that she be prepared beforehand. A mother of the Maker had to be made ready below, for the refashioning of what was shattered. And she had to be a virgin, so that, just as the first man had been fashioned from virgin earth, the refashioning would be accomplished through a virgin womb. And no entrance of pleasure, not even lawful pleasure, was to be so much as imagined in the birth of the Creator, for the birth that the Master consented to set free had been captive to pleasure. But who was worthy to serve this mystery? Who was worthy to become the Mother of God and lend flesh to him who owns the universe? Who, then, was worthy? Is it not clear that it was she who today sprouted so wondrously from Joachim and Anna, a fruitless root? We celebrate her birthday with splendour. Her birth is the prelude to the wonder of the greatest mystery, by which I mean the birth of the Word in the flesh, and it is for her sake that this public and divine festival has been assembled. It was necessary, truly necessary, that she who from her very swaddling clothes kept her body pure, her soul pure and her thoughts pure, beyond words, should be foreordained as Mother of the One who fashioned her. It was necessary that she who was brought to the temple as an infant and entered the inaccessible places should be seen as a living temple of the One who gave her a soul. It was necessary that she who was born from barren loins in a wondrous way, and who removed her parents' reproach, should also repair the failing of our forefathers. For the descendant was able to undo the ancestral defeat by bearing without a man the Saviour of the race and giving him a body. It was necessary that she who had beautifully shaped herself with the beauty of the soul

should appear as a chosen bride, resplendent for the heavenly bridegroom. It was necessary that she who had made herself a heaven, with the ways of the virtues for stars, should be recognized by all the faithful as the one from whom the Sun of righteousness rises. It was necessary that she who had once and for all dyed herself purple with the dye of virgin blood should become the royal robe of the King of all. O what a wonder! He whom all creation cannot contain, the virgin womb carries without being cramped. He on whom the Cherubim dare not gaze, the Virgin carries in arms of clay. The holy mountain comes forth from a desert and barren womb. From it the precious stone was cut without hands: the cornerstone, Christ our God, who shattered the precincts of the demons and the kingdoms of Hades, tyranny and all. The living, heavenly furnace is forged on earth. In it the Maker of the lump from which I am made bakes the first-fruits with divine fire, burns up the tares sown among them, and makes the whole into pure bread for himself [?]

But what could anyone say? What would anyone not feel as he sails across the sea of the Virgin's gifts and achievements? The mind fears and rejoices. It is still, and it leaps. It falls silent, then cries out. It shrinks and it expands, drawn now by fear and now by longing. As for me, I now give myself over to longing rather than fear, and, believe me, I would gladly have gone on before you in a full flood of words, however useless the stream of my speech, since the Virgin's wonders give me matter to brim over and overflow. I would do so above all because I see you eagerly opening your ears and fixing your whole mind on the praise of the Ever-Virgin. I would also be paying a debt of devotion, if indeed I have been initiated into the Virgin's mysteries. Nevertheless the hour summons us to other things, to another way of honouring the Virgin: I mean, to begin the mystical and bloodless sacrifice. For the honour paid to the Mother is the remembrance of the Son's voluntary sufferings. We are drawn toward it, and this is the most fitting time to celebrate it. But you, O Virgin and Mother of the Word, my propitiation and refuge, wondrously cultivated from a barren woman and more wondrously bearing for us the ear of life: intercede and mediate with your Son and our God. Cleanse those who sing your praises of every filth and every stain, and show them worthy of the heavenly bridal chamber, so that in their eternal portion they are illumined by the threefold light of the superessential Trinity and delight in its supernatural and ineffable visions. We ask this in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and might to the ages of ages. Amen.

By Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople: A Description of the New Church of the All-Holy Mother of God in the Palace, built under Basil the Macedonian. (Combefis, Manipulus rerum Constantinopolitanarum, p. 296.) I see that the gathering on this present day is a radiant one. No one could bring together such an assembly by human effort without the help of God.

So I welcome the delightful gifts of grace, and I rejoice and exult as I join the flock of Christ in its prosperity and joy. I know that the delight and gladness of this festival is not confined to us, and that its solemnity is offered to our common Master himself. For the more the splendour of a festival brings glory to us who celebrate it, the clearer the signs it gives of the Master's love. And when a festival does not commemorate something performed every year by custom, but inaugurates a new and newly revealed honour to God, will it not show all the more that it kindles divine love, and spread still further the dignity and renown of those who celebrate it? But why has so great a crowd run together and gathered? What is this festival? What has called us all together and stirred us? Shall I tell you? Or would it be better to give way to him and let him explain and teach the occasion of the festival, since he is both its sponsor and its wise architect? He is well able to set forth the matter in words, for he first fixed the patterns of these things in his soul and then, with all wisdom, raised on earth a work that no one can imitate. Tell us, then, O most Christ-loving and God-beloved of emperors, you who both surpass all your predecessors and lend them brilliant lustre by sharing their rank. Tell us why you have called us together, for as you see, your listeners are eager. Show us in your

and of Nicholas, who holds first place among the hierarchs, [?] … [?]tion of Holy Mary: At the same time this most beautiful and conspicuous church was also built [?] … which we have been accustomed to call the Basilica [?]. It was built in the name of our Saviour Jesus Christ, of Michael the first of the angels, and of Elijah the Tishbite. For he was repaying [?], as it were, Christ the Master for his kindness toward him, and Gabriel, the first of the angelic powers, and Elijah the Tishbite, the Zealot, who had also appeared as a messenger to his mother, announcing that her son would be raised to the throne. To their name and everlasting memory, and also to that of the Mother of God,

words what you have already displayed in your deeds. Have you once more set up victories and trophies over the barbarians? You have often entertained us kindly with such deeds, one after another. Is this why you have gathered us, both to gladden us and to send up common, public thanks to the Giver? Or have you made still other peoples tributary, and humbled some lofty, arrogant, foreign spirit, piously ascribing all your successes to the mighty hand of God? Or have you won subject cities, restoring some that had long lain in ruins, raising others from their very foundations, resettling others, and filling the borders of the state with people? Or have you been enriching your subjects and making them prosperous? Teach us, who look to you as the common eye of the world: for which of these have you called us together? Or are you keeping silent out of modesty, unwilling to recount your achievements to us, since praise would have to be woven in with them? And do you leave it to me, inspired by your works, to proclaim in speech the cause of this assembly? This, then, my friends, is a different rite and a different mystery today. Today a virginal temple is dedicated on earth, a dwelling worthy of the Mother of God, if anything in this world is. Today a virginal temple is dedicated on earth, a work of imperial magnificence, truly worthy of many hymns. This temple rises as another palace, divine and venerable, in the very midst of the palace. Set beside it and compared with it, the palace looks like a collection of private houses. Or rather, it flashes its own splendour around the palace, brightens it, and makes it far more stately than its former adornment did. Seeing it, you would say that it was not the work of human hands, but that some divine power beyond us had shaped its beauty. For splendid gateways have been built for the temple. Slabs of pure white marble, gleaming with a bright and graceful light, cover the whole façade. They are so even and smooth and fitted so closely together that they hide how they are laid against one another and where their edges meet, so that the whole seems a single continuous stone marked with straight lines. They beguile the imagination of those who see them, a new and most delightful marvel to behold. So they hold the eyes and draw them to themselves, and make the spectator unwilling to move on to the interior. Instead the visitor fills himself with the beautiful sight in the forecourt itself, fixes his eyes on what he sees, and stands as though rooted to the spot by the marvel. The myths make Orpheus the Thracian strike a lyre that moved lifeless things with its sounds. If we too were allowed to soar into myth and make the truth awesome [?], one might say that those who approach the forecourt are turned into trees by the marvel and transformed into the nature of plants, so hard is it for anyone who has once seen it to tear himself away.

When at last someone has barely torn himself away from there and looks into the sanctuary itself, how great a joy he is filled with, and with it what agitation and wonder! It is as though he has entered heaven itself, with nothing blocking his view from any side. The many beauties that appear everywhere shine around him like stars, and he is utterly astounded. Then it seems to him that everything else is in ecstasy and that the sanctuary itself is spinning around. For the variety of the spectacle on every side forces the spectator to turn in every direction and to keep moving, and he imagines that what he feels is happening in the thing he sees. Gold and silver cover most of the church. Gold is laid on in mosaic cubes, while silver is cut into plates and embossed, and each is applied to different parts. Here capitals are adorned; there are golden bands [?]; elsewhere gold is intertwined with chains. Or there is the holy table, a composition [?] more marvellous than gold. Silver is used at the little gates and doors [?] of the sanctuary, along with the surrounding colonnades [?], and on the cone-shaped canopy that stands over the holy table, together with its supporting columns and the ceiling beneath [?]. Wherever gold has not overspread or silver enclosed, a wonderful and delightful work of art in many-coloured marbles adorns the rest of the church. The floor has been worked by many-hued mosaic cubes into the shapes of animals and figures of other kinds, and the sight of it displays the wonderful skill of the craftsman. It shows that those famous artists, men like Phidias, Parrhasius, Praxiteles and Zeuxis, were mere children and makers of trifles in their art. If Democritus had seen the fine workmanship of the floor, I think he would have taken it as proof and said that his own atoms were close to being discovered and made visible. So completely is everything filled with won- (5) Or, "a composition more marvellous than gold." Constantine puts it thus: {The inner sanctuary of the church … with gold and silver and precious stones and pearls [?] … all of silver, with gold poured all over it, and with precious stones [?] … clothed in costly pearls, having their joining and structure [?].} The very altar table in Saint Sophia [?] … prospering [?].

-der. The architect of the sanctuary seems to me to have made only one mistake. He gathered all its beauties together into one and the same space, and so he does not let the spectator enjoy the sight undisturbed. One thing draws him away from another and distracts him, and nothing allows him to gaze his fill on what he sees. There is one thing I passed over that should have been mentioned first, for even in speech the marvel of this sanctuary will not let the speaker do his work in an orderly way. Let it be said now. On the ceiling itself there is an image of a man bearing the form of Christ, depicted in mosaic cubes of many colours. You would say that he was watching over the earth and planning its ordering and government, so precisely, as if inspired, has the painter expressed the Creator's care for us even in mere shapes and colours. In the circular sections of the dome around the ceiling a throng of angels is depicted, forming the escort of our common Master. The apse that rises above the altar shines with the image of the Virgin. She stretches out her stainless hands on our behalf and obtains safety for the emperor and valiant victories over his enemies. A choir of apostles and martyrs, and of prophets and patriarchs as well, fills the whole church with their images and beautifies it. One of them, though silent, cries aloud through the words he once uttered: "How lovely are your dwellings, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord." Another cries: "How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God." And perhaps someone who is not one of ours and is not depicted here would also cry out, unwillingly proclaiming our things divine: "How fair are your houses, O Jacob, and your tents, O Israel! Like gardens beside rivers, and like the tents that the Lord pitched, and not man." Long ago a tabernacle was built for Moses, who saw God, at God's command, so that sacrifice might be offered to God to make atonement for sins. Later the temple in Jerusalem was built for King Solomon, a delightful work that eclipsed everything before it in beauty, size and costliness. But those works fall as far short of the church now built by our faithful and great emperor as shadow and type fall short of the truth and the realities themselves. This is not only because this church belongs to grace and the Spirit while they belonged to the law and the letter, but also because they take second place in beauty and in every other kind of craftsmanship and skill. And why should anyone try, in so brief a speech, to go through the wonders of this famous sanctuary? Even sight itself, which leaves the other senses far behind in swiftness, is

clearly unable to take them in, even over a long time. So I rejoice no less if my speech has fallen short than if it had reached the full measure of an adequate description. For my purpose was not to display my power as a speaker, but to show that this church is the most beautiful and lovely of all, and that it surpasses the rules of description. But now let the course of my speech turn and direct itself to you, the cause of this assembly. Rejoice, then, O emperor, favoured by God's grace and most beloved of God. Renew your youth in body and soul as you flourish in good works, and celebrate the dedication of this famous church, the work of your wisdom and your hand. "Bend your bow, prosper and reign, for the sake of truth and meekness and righteousness." For the right hand of the Most High guides you, as can plainly be seen, and will go on guiding you. It is the hand of him who created you and anointed you from your very cradle as king of his own chosen people. You too, rejoice with him and be renewed with him, the ornament of all the Caesars the sun has ever looked upon, who surpass your predecessors in wisdom and understanding. You were chosen [?] by divine decree to receive so great an office, not because you sought it or won it by human intrigue. Rejoice, then, and be renewed together with him who has taken you as partner and sharer of his reign, for the common safety of his subjects and as [?] of his goodwill toward you and his most sincere love. For through the two of you the Trinity, piously served and worshipped, extends and conveys its providence to all, and wisely steers and governs the subjects. Rejoice, you too, Fathers of the Senate, venerable and reverend grey heads, as you are renewed together with our faithful, great and august emperor and with the Caesar, who celebrates with you the dedication of this famous church. The whole company of priests and high priests rejoices and makes merry too, and counts the consecration of this church as their own glory and boast. Rejoice and dance together, you also, the rest of this God-loving gathering, as you see the church of the Virgin, another heaven on earth, dedicated today. By her intercessions may we all attain that blessed and endless grace and exultation in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and might, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.
